slides.title: Regularization
slides.body:
Regularization often works by trading an increase in bias for a reduction of variance. 
An effective regularizer reduces variance while not increasing bias.

Higher variance, lower bias 
Bad generalization

Lower variance, higher bias 
Good generalization

Regularize

slides.title: L1 and L2 Regularization
slides.notes:
The key difference between these techniques is that L1 shrinks the less important feature’s coefficients to zero thus, removing some feature altogether. So, this works well for feature selection in case we have a huge number of features.

L2 regularization out-of-the-box
Yes, pytorch optimizers have a parameter called weight_decay which corresponds to the L2 regularization factor:
sgd = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), weight_decay=weight_decay)

L1 regularization implementation
There is no analogous argument for L1, however this is straightforward to implement manually:
loss = loss_fn(outputs, labels)
l1_lambda = 0.001
l1_norm = sum(torch.linalg.norm(p, 1) for p in model.parameters())

loss = loss + l1_lambda * l1_norm

The equivalent manual implementation of L2 would be:
l2_norm = sum(torch.linalg.norm(p, 2) for p in model.parameters())

slides.title: The Covariate Shift Problem
slides.body:
Problem: the distribution of a layer's inputs changes during training.
Consequences: 
More difficult for the model to learn effectively
Neurons become sensitive to the specific characteristics of the training data.
Reduced learning speed

slides.title: Batch Normalization Goals
slides.body:
Normalize Activations: Batch normalization normalizes the inputs within each mini-batch during training.
Mitigate Covariate Shift: By reducing the internal covariate shift, batch normalization helps maintain a stable distribution of inputs to layers.
slides.notes:
Compute Batch Statistics: During training, for each mini-batch of data fed into the network, batch normalization computes the mean and standard deviation of the activations along each feature dimension.
Normalize: Then, it normalizes the activations using these batch statistics, subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation.
Scale and Shift: Batch normalization introduces two learnable parameters per feature dimension: a scaling parameter (gamma) and a shifting parameter (beta). After normalization, the activations are scaled by gamma and shifted by beta.

slides.title: Batch Normalization
slides.body:
Challenge?
behaviour of ML/DL algorithms can change when the input distribution changes
In DL: specifically concerned with the change in the distribution of the inputs to the inner nodes within a network (output or activations of one layer, is the input for the next etc. => the input distribution changes with each step)
Solution?
Batch normalization (batchnorm) proposes a technique to help coordinate the update for multiple layers in the model
How?
standardizing the activations of each input variable (per minibatch) by calculating the mean and standard deviation of each input variable to a layer (per mini-batch)
slides.notes:
Challenge:
In DL: change in the distribution of the inputs to the inner nodes within a network => a NN changes the weights of each layer over the course of training (backprop), this means that the activations of each layer change as well! The activations of the previous layer are the input for the next one, each layer in the NN is faced with a situation where the input distribution changes with each step.
The basic idea behind batch normalization is to limit covariate shift by normalizing the activations of each layer (transforming the inputs to be mean 0 and unit variance). This, supposedly, allows each layer to learn on a more stable distribution of inputs, and would thus accelerate the training of the network.

slides.title: Other forms of Normalization
slides.notes: 1. Batch Normalization (BN): Calculates mean and variance across the Batch and Spatial dimensions for each channel independently. Best for: Standard CNNs and large-scale computer vision tasks. Pros: Accelerates training; provides slight regularization. Cons: Highly dependent on batch size; fails when the batch size is small (e.g., ) because the statistics become noisy. 2. Layer Normalization (LN): Calculates mean and variance across the Channel and Spatial dimensions for each individual image in the batch. Best for: RNNs, Transformers (NLP), and Reinforcement Learning. Pros: Independent of batch size; works well with sequential data where sequence lengths vary. Cons: Generally performs worse than BN in standard vision tasks. 3. Instance Normalization (IN): Calculates mean and variance across the Spatial dimensions only, for each channel and each image independently. Best for: Style Transfer, GANs, and Image Generation. Pros: Removes instance-specific "style" or contrast, focusing on the content of the image. Cons: Discards global information that might be useful for classification. 4. Group Normalization (GN): A middle ground between LN and IN. It divides channels into groups and normalizes within those groups. Best for: Object Detection, Segmentation, and high-resolution tasks where small batch sizes are forced by memory limits. Pros: Performance is stable regardless of batch size; often outperforms BN when batch sizes are very small. Cons: Requires choosing a hyperparameter (number of groups).
